{{Short description|Any of several recursively-defined integer sequences}}
In [[mathematics]], a '''Hofstadter sequence''' is a member of a family of related [[integer sequence]]s defined by non-linear [[recurrence relation]]s.

==Sequences presented in ''Gödel, Escher, Bach: an Eternal Golden Braid''==
The first Hofstadter sequences were described by [[Douglas Hofstadter|Douglas Richard Hofstadter]] in his book ''[[Gödel, Escher, Bach]]''. In order of their presentation in chapter III on figures and background (Figure-Figure sequence) and chapter V on recursive structures and processes (remaining sequences), these sequences are:

===Hofstadter Figure-Figure sequences===
The Hofstadter Figure-Figure (R and S) sequences are a pair of [[Lambek–Moser theorem|complementary integer sequences]] defined as follows:<ref>{{harvp|Hofstadter|1980|p=73}}</ref><ref>{{mathworld|urlname = HofstadterFigure-FigureSequence |title = Hofstadter Figure-Figure Sequence}}</ref>
: <math>
\begin{align}
 R(1) &= 1,\ S(1) = 2; \\
 R(n) &= R(n - 1) + S(n - 1), \quad n > 1,
\end{align}
</math>
with the sequence <math>S(n)</math> defined as a strictly increasing series of positive integers not present in <math>R(n)</math>. The first few terms of these sequences are
: ''R'': 1, 3, 7, 12, 18, 26, 35, 45, 56, 69, 83, 98, 114, 131, 150, 170, 191, 213, 236, 260,&nbsp;... {{OEIS|id=A005228}}
: ''S'': 2, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 11, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 19, 20, 21, 22, 23, 24, 25,&nbsp;... {{OEIS|id=A030124}}

===Hofstadter G sequence===
The Hofstadter G sequence is defined as follows:<ref name=hof137>{{harvp|Hofstadter|1980|p=137}}</ref><ref>{{mathworld|urlname = HofstadterG-Sequence |title = Hofstadter G-Sequence}}</ref>
: <math>
\begin{align}
 G(0)& = 0, \\
 G(n)& = n - G\big(G(n - 1)\big), \quad n > 0.
\end{align}
</math>

The first few terms of this sequence are
: 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 5, 6, 6, 7, 8, 8, 9, 9, 10, 11, 11, 12, 12,&nbsp;... {{OEIS|id=A005206}}

===Hofstadter H sequence===
The Hofstadter H sequence is defined as follows:<ref name=hof137 /><ref>{{mathworld|urlname = HofstadterH-Sequence |title = Hofstadter H-Sequence}}</ref>
: <math>
\begin{align}
 H(0) &= 0, \\
 H(n) &= n - H\Big(H\big(H(n - 1)\big)\Big), \quad n > 0.
\end{align}
</math>

The first few terms of this sequence are
: 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 4, 4, 5, 5, 6, 7, 7, 8, 9, 10, 10, 11, 12, 13, 13, 14,&nbsp;... {{OEIS|id=A005374}}

===Hofstadter Female and Male sequences===
The Hofstadter Female (''F'') and Male (''M'') sequences are defined as follows:<ref name=hof137 /><ref>{{mathworld|urlname = HofstadterMale-FemaleSequences |title = Hofstadter Male-Female Sequences}}</ref>
: <math>
\begin{align}
 F(0) &= 1,\ M(0) = 0; \\
 F(n) &= n - M\big(F(n - 1)\big), \quad n > 0, \\
 M(n) &= n - F\big(M(n - 1)\big), \quad n > 0.
\end{align}
</math>

The first few terms of these sequences are
: ''F'': 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 5, 5, 6, 6, 7, 8, 8, 9, 9, 10, 11, 11, 12, 13,&nbsp;... {{OEIS|id=A005378}}
: ''M'': 0, 0, 1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 4, 5, 6, 6, 7, 7, 8, 9, 9, 10, 11, 11, 12, 12,&nbsp;... {{OEIS|id=A005379}}

===Hofstadter Q sequence===
The Hofstadter Q sequence is defined as follows:<ref name=hof137 /><ref>{{mathworld|urlname = HofstadtersQ-Sequence |title = Hofstadter's Q-Sequence}}</ref>
: <math>
\begin{align}
 Q(1) &= Q(2) = 1, \\
 Q(n) &= Q\big(n - Q(n - 1)\big) + Q\big(n - Q(n - 2)\big), \quad n > 2.
\end{align}
</math>

The first few terms of the sequence are
: 1, 1, 2, 3, 3, 4, 5, 5, 6, 6, 6, 8, 8, 8, 10, 9, 10, 11, 11, 12,&nbsp;... {{OEIS|id=A005185}}

Hofstadter named the terms of the sequence "Q numbers";<ref name=hof137 /> thus the Q number of 6 is 4. The presentation of the Q sequence in Hofstadter's book is actually the first known mention of a [[meta-Fibonacci sequence]] in literature.<ref>{{harvp|Emerson|2006|pp=1, 7}}</ref>

While the terms of the [[Fibonacci sequence]] are determined by summing the two preceding terms, the two preceding terms of a Q number determine how far to go back in the Q sequence to find the two terms to be summed. The indices of the summation terms thus depend on the Q sequence itself.

''Q''(1), the first element of the sequence, is never one of the two terms being added to produce a later element; it is involved only within an index in the calculation of ''Q''(3).<ref>{{harvp|Pinn|1999|pp=5–6}}</ref>

Although the terms of the Q sequence seem to flow chaotically,<ref name=hof137 /><ref name="pin3">{{harvp|Pinn|1999|p=3}}</ref><ref>{{harvp|Pinn|2000|p=1}}</ref><ref name="Emerson 2006 p 7">{{harvp|Emerson|2006|p=7}}</ref> like many meta-Fibonacci sequences, its terms can be grouped into blocks of successive generations.<ref>{{harvp|Pinn|1999|pp=3–4}}</ref><ref>{{harvp|Balamohan|Kuznetsov|Tanny|2007|p=19}}</ref> In case of the Q sequence, the ''k''-th generation has 2<sup>''k''</sup> members.<ref>{{harvp|Pinn|1999|loc=Abstract, p. 8}}</ref> Furthermore, with ''g'' being the generation that a Q number belongs to, the two terms to be summed to calculate the Q number, called its parents, reside by far mostly in generation ''g''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;1 and only a few in generation ''g''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;2, but never in an even older generation.<ref>{{harvp|Pinn|1999|pp=4–5}}</ref>

Most of these findings are empirical observations, since virtually nothing has been [[mathematical proof|proved]] about the ''Q'' sequence so far.<ref name="pin2">{{harvp|Pinn|1999|p=2}}</ref><ref>{{harvp|Pinn|2000|p=3}}</ref><ref name="bal2">{{harvp|Balamohan|Kuznetsov|Tanny|2007|p=2}}</ref> It is specifically unknown whether the sequence is well-defined for all ''n''; that is, whether the sequence "dies" at some point because its generation rule tries to refer to terms which would conceptually sit left of the first term ''Q''(1).<ref name="Emerson 2006 p 7"/><ref name=pin2 /><ref name=bal2 />

==Generalizations of the ''Q'' sequence==
===Hofstadter–Huber ''Q''<sub>''r'',''s''</sub>(''n'') family===
20 years after Hofstadter first described the ''Q'' sequence, he and [[Greg Huber]] used the character ''Q'' to name the generalization of the ''Q'' sequence toward a family of sequences, and renamed the original ''Q'' sequence of his book to ''U'' sequence.<ref name=bal2 />

The original ''Q'' sequence is generalized by replacing ''n''&nbsp;−&nbsp;1 and ''n''&nbsp;−&nbsp;2 by ''n''&nbsp;−&nbsp;''r'' and ''n''&nbsp;−&nbsp;''s'', respectively.<ref name=bal2 />

This leads to the sequence family

:<math>Q_{r,s}(n) = \begin{cases}
1 , \quad 1 \le n \le s, \\
Q_{r,s}(n-Q_{r,s}(n-r))+Q_{r,s}(n-Q_{r,s}(n-s)), \quad n > s,
\end{cases}</math>

where ''s''&nbsp;≥&nbsp;2 and ''r''&nbsp;<&nbsp;''s''.

With (''r'',''s'') = (1,2), the original ''Q'' sequence is a member of this family. So far, only three sequences of the family ''Q''<sub>''r'',''s''</sub> are known, namely the ''U'' sequence with (''r'',''s'') = (1,2) (which is the original ''Q'' sequence);<ref name=bal2 /> the ''V'' sequence with (''r'',''s'') = (1,4);<ref>{{harvp|Balamohan|Kuznetsov|Tanny|2007|loc=full article}}</ref> and the W sequence with (''r'',''s'') = (2,4).<ref name=bal2 /> Only the V sequence, which does not behave as chaotically as the others, is proven not to "die".<ref name=bal2 /> Similar to the original ''Q'' sequence, virtually nothing has been proved rigorously about the W sequence to date.<ref name=bal2 />

The first few terms of the V sequence are

:1, 1, 1, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 5, 6, 6, 7, 8, 8, 9, 9, 10, 11, 11, 11, ... {{OEIS|id=A063882}}

The first few terms of the W sequence are

:1, 1, 1, 1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 7, 5, 3, 8, 9, 11, 12, 9, 9, 13, 11, 9, ... {{OEIS|id=A087777}}

For other values (''r'',''s'') the sequences sooner or later "die" i.e. there exists an ''n'' for which ''Q''<sub>''r'',''s''</sub>(''n'') is undefined because ''n''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;''Q''<sub>''r'',''s''</sub>(''n''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;''r'')&nbsp;<&nbsp;1.<ref name=bal2 />

===Pinn ''F''<sub>''i'',''j''</sub>(''n'') family===
In 1998, [[Klaus Pinn]], scientist at [[University of Münster]] (Germany) and in close communication with Hofstadter, suggested another generalization of Hofstadter's ''Q'' sequence which Pinn called ''F'' sequences.<ref name="pin16">{{harvp|Pinn|2000|p=16}}</ref>

The family of Pinn ''F''<sub>''i'',''j''</sub> sequences is defined as follows:

:<math>
F_{i,j}(n) =
\begin{cases}
1 , \quad n=1,2, \\
F_{i,j}(n-i-F_{i,j}(n-1))+F_{i,j}(n-j-F_{i,j}(n-2)), \quad n > 2.
\end{cases}
</math>

Thus Pinn introduced additional constants ''i'' and ''j'' which shift the index of the terms of the summation conceptually to the left (that is, closer to start of the sequence).<ref name=pin16 />

Only ''F'' sequences with (''i'',''j'') = (0,0), (0,1), (1,0), and (1,1), the first of which represents the original ''Q'' sequence, appear to be well-defined.<ref name=pin16 /> Unlike ''Q''(1), the first elements of the Pinn ''F''<sub>''i'',''j''</sub>(''n'') sequences are terms of summations in calculating later elements of the sequences when any of the additional constants is&nbsp;1.

The first few terms of the Pinn ''F''<sub>0,1</sub> sequence are

:1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 4, 4, 5, 6, 6, 7, 8, 8, 8, 8, 9, 10, 10, 11, ... {{OEIS|id=A046699}}

==Hofstadter–Conway $10,000 sequence==
The Hofstadter–Conway $10,000 sequence is defined as follows<ref>{{mathworld|urlname = Hofstadter-Conway10000-DollarSequence |title = Hofstadter-Conway $10,000 Sequence}}</ref>
<math display=block>
 \begin{align}
  a(1) &= a(2) = 1, \\
  a(n) &= a\big(a(n - 1)\big) + a\big(n - a(n - 1)\big), \quad n > 2.
 \end{align}
</math>

The first few terms of this sequence are

: 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 4, 4, 5, 6, 7, 7, 8, 8, 8, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, ... {{OEIS|id=A004001}}

The values <math>a(n)/n</math> converge to 1/2, and this sequence acquired its name because [[John Horton Conway]] offered a prize of $10,000 to anyone who could determine its [[rate of convergence]]. The prize, since reduced to $1,000, was claimed by [[Colin L. Mallows]], who proved that<ref>{{cite web | url = http://el.media.mit.edu/logo-foundation/resources/papers/pdf/easy_as_11223.pdf | title = Easy as 1 1 2 2 3 | first = Michael | last = Tempel }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last=Mallows |first=Colin L. |doi=10.2307/2324028 |issue=1 |journal=[[The American Mathematical Monthly]] |jstor=2324028 |mr=1083608 |pages=5–20 |title=Conway's challenge sequence |volume=98 |year=1991}}</ref>
<math display=block>
\left|\frac{a(n)}{n} - \frac{1}{2}\right| = O\!\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{\log n}}\right).
</math>
In private communication with [[Klaus Pinn]], Hofstadter later claimed that he had found the sequence and its structure about 10–15 years before Conway posed his challenge.<ref name=pin3 />
